note: Postcard spots for web/postcards.js, written by pipeline/postcards.py from cities/<id>/postcards.json.

any: Bob's Peak, by the top of the gondola. Lake Wakatipu bends away below like a river that forgot to stop.
From the Skyline terrace: the town, the bay, the Gardens on their point, and the Remarkables across the lake.
dusk: The Remarkables hold the last light for a few minutes after the town has lost it. The whole terrace went quiet to watch.

any: The point of the Queenstown Gardens, with the Remarkables over the trees. Ten minutes' walk from the main street and nobody here.
Marine Parade, on the bay. The water is so clear at the edge that the stones look dry, and the old steamer berths just along the shore.
St Peter's, a stone church with a small spire, a street back from the lake. Its door was open.
Sat where Mrs Macquarie used to sit and watch for ships. From her bench the sails and the bridge line up as if somebody planned it.
dusk: The sun goes down behind the bridge from here. Everyone on the point stopped talking for about a minute.
night: The sails are lit and the bridge is a string of lamps. I stayed on the point longer than I meant to.

any: Up on the Cahill Walk, over the station. The whole quay is below, ferries in and out, and the bridge is straight ahead.
The sails are bigger than the photographs say, and not quite white: close up, the tiles are cream and they shine.
dusk: Last light on the shells. The steps were still warm when I sat down on them.

any: Under the bridge at Dawes Point. You hear a train cross before you see it, and the whole deck hums.
Circular Quay from the west side. A ferry leaves every few minutes, and each one swings past the Opera House on its way out.
A table by the sea wall at the Opera Bar, the bridge across the water. The gulls here watch every chip.
night: The bridge lit from end to end, and its lights broken up on the water. Nobody at the bar was in a hurry.

any: Kyoto Tower, straight out of the station. 131 metres, and nothing else in the city comes close. People here say it is how they know they are home.

kyoto.name: Higashi Honganji, the Founder's Hall Gate

any: The Founder's Hall Gate of Higashi Honganji, on Karasuma-dori. It is so large that the street in front of it feels like part of the temple.
Through the gate, the Founder's Hall. One of the largest wooden buildings there is, and people cross its forecourt quietly without being asked.
Nishi Hongwanji, a few streets west of its sister temple. A great tiled roof, a ginkgo by the hall, and hardly anyone here.
The gravel avenues of the Imperial Palace gardens. They are wide enough for a procession, and mostly it is one person on a bicycle.
Yasaka Pagoda at the top of the stone street: five storeys, 46 metres, rebuilt in 1440. Every photograph of Kyoto has it in somewhere, and now mine does.
dusk: Dusk on Yasaka-dori. The pagoda goes dark against the sky and the street empties in ten minutes.

any: The Nio Gate of Kiyomizu-dera, vermilion at the top of the hill. After the climb through the lanes, it is the first thing that lets you stop.
From the Okunoin: the whole Main Hall on its pillars, the stage hanging over the trees, the city behind. This is the photograph everyone takes. I took it too.
On the stage of Kiyomizu. Hinoki boards, great pillars underneath and not a single nail, and about thirteen metres down to the treetops.
The South Gate of Yasaka Shrine in Gion. The proper way in, people here say, though most of us come by the gate on the main street.
The main hall of Yasaka Shrine, vermilion and white. Somebody is always ringing the bell and clapping twice.
The approach to Fushimi Inari from the station. You see the first great torii from the street, and everybody walks a little faster.
The Romon, the shrine's tower gate. Hideyoshi gave it in 1589, they say in thanks for his mother getting well. Two stone foxes keep it.
Inside the Senbon Torii. Two tunnels side by side, and you keep to the right one going up. In here even the air looks orange.
A side path up the mountain, away from the crowd. Each gate has a name on its back: the person or the company that gave it.
Higher up, the forest comes in close and the gates go on. Fewer people, more birds, and the steps do not stop.

tetsugaku.name: The Philosopher's Path, the north end

any: The north end of the Philosopher's Path. A professor used to walk here every day to think. I mostly thought about lunch.
On the Philosopher's Path. The canal beside it runs north, which feels wrong in Kyoto, and the trees lean in from both banks.
By Eikan-do, under the eastern hills. The temple is known for its maples, and the hill behind it is nothing but trees.
The Sanmon of Nanzen-ji through the trees. A gate two storeys tall with a balcony, standing in a wood as if it grew there.
The Keage Incline. Boats once rode up this slope on rail cars to the canal above. Now people walk between the rails.
The crossing at Kamakurakokomae, from the hill road. The road drops to the rails, and past the rails there is only the sea.
Kamakurakokomae Station. One platform, one track, and the whole of Sagami Bay in front of it, with Enoshima to the west.
Shichirigahama. Dark sand, a long swell coming in, and Enoshima lying on the horizon.
Inamuragasaki. From the cape the coast road runs west along the bay, all the way to Enoshima.
dusk: People come to the cape for this hour: Enoshima goes black against the sky, and on a clear evening Fuji stands behind it.

any: The sea wall at Koshigoe's fishing harbour. Enoshima is so near from here that you could row to it.
Tokyo Station from the Marunouchi side. Red brick from 1914, the domes it lost in the war put back in 2012, and glass towers all round it.
Nijubashi, the stone bridge to the Palace. The moat is so still that the bridge is drawn twice.
Marunouchi Naka-dori, between the towers. A canyon of glass at street level, and behind every window somebody is working.
Ginza. Wide pavements, signs stacked up the sides of the buildings, and people who dress to walk here.
night: Ginza after dark. The signs do the work of streetlamps, and nobody looks at them.

any: Kabuki-za. White walls, red lanterns and a curved gable, with an office tower growing out of its back.
Tokyo Tower from below: 333 metres of orange and white steel. It looks close from everywhere and is never as close as it looks.
night: Tokyo Tower lit up. From its foot you have to lean right back to see the top.

any: The scramble. When the lights change, up to three thousand people cross at once from every corner, and nobody touches anybody.
Hachiko. He met his master here every evening, and kept coming for almost ten years after his master died. Tokyo still says 'meet at Hachiko'.
The mouth of Center Gai. Ramen, arcades, a screen on every wall, and a sign that calls it Basketball Street.
SHIBUYA SKY, 229 metres up, behind a wall of glass. The city goes on until it turns into haze.
night: From the roof after dark. Tokyo has no edge: the lights just get smaller until they stop.

any: Chiyo-no-yu in Sangenjaya, a neighbourhood bathhouse. The curtain says ゆ, hot water, and two vending machines keep the door company.
Omotesando, the zelkova avenue. Straight as a ruler, and roofed with leaves.
Past the arch, Ichibangai runs north between the signs. Every doorway is somebody's idea of a good night out.
The red arch of Kabukicho Ichibangai. It has stood at the mouth of the street since 1969.
night: Kabukicho's arch with its bulbs on. Everything behind it is a sign for something.

any: The head over Central Road. Twelve metres of it on a terrace eight floors up, glaring down the street since 2015.
Shinjuku Gyoen, by the pond. The towers stand behind the trees and none of their noise gets in.
The footbridge at Shinanomachi. The tower with the clock stands on the skyline, small and exact.
